comments.author: @tommymarshall69
comments.text:
I'm a long-time Warp user too--it's a fantastic terminal, and at the very least is a massive time-saver for anyone who isn't a shell wizard. HOWEVER, your video was a little misleading when you said that the CLI tools like Claude Code or Codex are for people who want to go all in on one model. They're also great for people who want the opposite, because you can sign up for the cheapest available pay-as-you-go usage for each of them and seamlessly switch between model providers in the terminal and even run different models in parallel and even *compose* models from different providers by having one coding agent pass off a task to another (which allows you to delegate specific tasks and sub-tasks based on the relative strengths and weaknesses of the different models and model providers).

The reality is that you can sign up for "pay as you go" pricing with any of the CLI tools and pay for only what you use, and the experience is identical except you only pay for what you use. The main advantage of paying for a subscription from a foundation model provider like OpenAI or Anthropic is that you also get usage for their GUI chat apps bundled in. If you're only or mainly using the CLI tool (and honestly there isn't much reason to stick to the GUIs once you're used to the CLI version), then you don't need the subscription at all, or you can pay the lowest tier like $20 a month to retain access to the GUI version for everyday crap and use the CLI on a pay-for-what-you-use basis.

And the beauty of the CLI tools is that all the big frontier model providers have them. You have Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, and you can even use Grok via a free open-source 3rd-party CLI which is basically just as good as if Grok made their own.

AND—get this—you can actually have one company's CLI agent use another company's CLI agent! For example, if you have both the Claude Code CLI and the Gemini CLI installed, you can actually ask Claude to invoke gemini itself in a bash command and delegate a task to it by writing a prompt for you! I don't know whether you can do stuff like this with Warp, but my sense is that Warp basically handles a lot of the design and optimisation of agents for you, which is fine but it also means you have less control over the design of your agent workflows. For well-worn tasks like web development, Warp is probably going to do basically as good a job as you would do manually, but for anything beyond fairly commonplace software dev tasks you're probably going to want more control. And IMO you're going to be able to do more interesting things and unlock more powerful uses than you'll get if you have Warp do all of it for you.

Warp is already the king of AI terminals, so it's amazing at writing terminal commands and doing terminal operations. But when it comes to AI-assisted coding, if you want to code something with next to no software dev experience, Warp is what you want, because you can literally just use your words to have it make something for you. But if you want more control than that, my recommendation would be to use the CLI tools within Warp itself. Warp has a decent free tier, and if all you use it for is writing bash commands then the free tier or the lowest paid tier will probably cover you for that. The Warp UI is awesome, and you get all of that on the free tier--you only pay if you want to get AI usage. Then you set up API credentials on all the model providers you want to use, top them up (you can start with literally a few bucks each which will give you more than enough usage to test them each out very thoroughly).

The pay-per-month usage, direct from model providers, is way more economical for the vast majority of users. The video is right that, if you're going super hard on one company's models every day, then the subscriptions may well be worth it. But you have to be making not only heavy but consistently heavy use of that one company's models in order to make it worth it, and honestly with the pace of change and as company's continuously release models outdoing their competitors, you're going to want to be able to switch without having to futz with subscriptions. And I'd predict that a lot of users have significant variance in the volume of AI use on a day-to-day basis, in which case you're much better off doing pay-as-you-go. 

Sorry, this ended up being longer than I anticipated--but I've been researching this stuff heavily for the past few days and I just wanted to point all this out because there's a lot of missing nuance here, and I think you massively understate the case for the CLI tools. 

Also, if you're someone who loves the IDE, you can just use the CLI tools in the IDE terminal! VSCode also has plugins for Codex and Claude where you have a little chat window off to the side and you can ask it to make changes to your code, and they're pretty good, so you don't even have to use the command line if you really don't want to. I still think you'll find the CLI tools have the most power, though, and if you're allergic to the command line I highly recommend pushing through your distaste and giving these a go!

comments.text:
CodeWithHarry,I graduated from engineering in the late 90s. From a city most of you haven't heard of. No IIT. No NIT. No "coding since class 8" backstory.

My "placement preparation" was a photocopy of Balagurusamy and a prayer.

Nobody in my family had ever worked in software. Nobody in my college had ever worked at a product company. My professors were teaching C++ from textbooks that still referenced Turbo C. The placement cell's entire strategy was: "companies aa rahe hain, form bhar do."

I filled the form. I got a job. And then I spent the next several years realizing that getting the job was the easy part — surviving and growing in the industry was where the real confusion began.

What is this "Agile" thing everyone keeps talking about? Why does my manager keep saying "take ownership" but won't let me make decisions? What is the actual difference between a service company and a product company beyond the salary? Why did nobody tell me that the skills that get you hired are completely different from the skills that get you promoted?

I figured it out. Slowly. Painfully. By making mistakes that were entirely avoidable if someone had just sat me down and explained how this industry actually works.

My co-author Brij Purohit has a nearly identical story. Different college, different city, same confusion. Same years of trial and error learning things that should have been taught.

Between us, we've spent about 25 years in this industry. We've hired freshers. We've watched talented kids from tier-2 and tier-3 colleges flame out — not because they couldn't code, but because nobody told them what the game actually looks like. We've seen students mass-apply to service companies because they genuinely didn't know other options existed. We've seen final year students who could solve dynamic programming problems but couldn't explain what a product manager does, or what happens in a sprint retrospective, or why their dream company rejected them despite them "clearing the coding round."

This isn't a talent problem. It's an information problem.

If you're at IIT Bombay or BITS Pilani, you're swimming in information. Your seniors are at Google and Microsoft. Your alumni network answers DMs. Your placement cell has relationships with companies most students don't even know exist. You have access to context that makes the whole picture legible.

If you're at an engineering college in Bhopal or Nagpur or Ranchi or Lucknow, you're not dumb. You're not less capable. You're just operating with a fraction of the information. And in this industry, information asymmetry is the silent killer of careers.

That's why we wrote this book.

"Cracking the Indian Software Industry" isn't a DSA guide. It isn't "100 interview questions." There are enough of those. This book is the conversation you'd have with a senior engineer who's been in the industry for decades and is willing to tell you the stuff that doesn't show up in YouTube tutorials:

How the Indian software industry actually works — the ecosystem, the business models, the hiring patterns, the career paths nobody maps out for you

What companies actually evaluate beyond your coding skills, and why "culture fit" isn't the meaningless buzzword you think it is

How to think about your career as a system, not a series of disconnected placement drives

What changes when AI and automation reshape entry-level roles — because that's not a future problem, that's a right now problem

That last point is something I want to be direct about. The entry-level software job market in India is shifting under your feet. Mass hiring patterns are changing. Companies that used to hire 10,000 freshers are hiring 2,000 and expecting each one to do more from day one.
